groups.title: Express Routing & Middleware
groups.question: Explain how a request travels through an Express app, from arriving to getting a response.

followUps.The Middleware Pipeline: What happens if a middleware neither responds nor calls next()?
followUps.Router — Route Parameters & Query String: When does data belong in a route parameter like /books/:id, and when in a query string?

evidence.text: Each request passes through the middleware functions in the order they were registered.
Each middleware must either send a response or call next() to pass the request on.
If it does neither, the request hangs until the client times out.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (middleware, next()) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says Express moves to the next middleware automatically when a function returns.

evidence.text: Route parameters identify a specific resource, like the id in /books/:id.
Query strings carry optional filters, sorting or paging, like ?page=2&author=x.
Optional filters in the path make brittle URLs, while identity in the query string hides what the resource is.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (route params, query string) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says route parameters and query strings are interchangeable.

groups.title: REST API Design
groups.question: Explain how you would design the endpoints for a books API, and how you keep bad input out.

followUps.Resource Naming & HTTP Verbs: Why is /books with POST better than /createBook?
followUps.Input Validation with Zod or Joi: Why validate the request body at the route, before any business logic runs?

evidence.text: URLs name resources with nouns, usually plural: /books, /books/:id.
The action comes from the HTTP method (POST creates, GET reads, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes), not from the URL.
That keeps the API predictable and consistent, and plays well with caching and tooling.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (REST, nouns, verbs) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says each action should get its own URL, like /createBook.

evidence.text: Request input is checked against a schema at the route, before any business logic runs.
Bad input is rejected with a clear 400 error instead of failing deeper with a 500 or corrupting data.
Client input can't be trusted, and validating it also blocks injection and type errors.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Zod, Joi, validation) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says validating in the frontend is enough, so the server doesn't need to check.

groups.title: Error Handling & Logging
groups.question: Explain how your API should handle errors and record what happened on each request.

followUps.Centralized Error-Handling Middleware: What makes Express treat a middleware as an error handler, and why have just one?
followUps.Request Logging with morgan: Which details should an access log record so you can find the endpoint that returns 500s?

evidence.text: Express treats middleware with four arguments (err, req, res, next) as an error handler.
Errors reach it through next(err) or thrown/rejected errors, and it is registered after the routes.
One central handler gives every error the same response shape and status codes, and logs it in one place.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (error middleware, next(err)) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the error handler should be registered before the routes.

evidence.text: Each request's method, path, status code and response time is logged.
Then you can filter or count 500s per endpoint and see which one is failing or slow.
A request id or timestamp ties the access log line to other logs about the same request.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (morgan, logging) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says logging the error message alone is enough to find the failing endpoint.

groups.title: API Structure & Versioning
groups.question: Explain how you would organize an API's code as it grows, and how you ship breaking changes.

followUps.Controller Pattern — Separating Routes f: Why move logic out of route callbacks, and how does that help testing?
followUps.API Versioning Strategies: How does putting /v1 in the URL let you ship a breaking change without breaking existing clients?

evidence.text: Routes only map URLs to functions; the logic lives in controllers or services.
Logic separated from HTTP can be unit-tested directly, without starting a server.
Route files stay short and easy to scan.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (controllers, MVC) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the pattern exists mainly to make the API run faster.

evidence.text: /v1 and /v2 run side by side, so existing clients keep using v1 unchanged.
Breaking changes go only into the new version, and clients move over when they are ready.
The old version is deprecated with notice and removed later.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (versioning, /v1) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the version must be bumped for every change, including non-breaking ones.
